bridge: B04 introduced virtual machines and S06 introduced permission. Use the fictional cloud account diagram rather than creating live resources.
teaching:
### Divide the responsibilities

The provider and customer share responsibilities differently for virtual machines, managed databases and application platforms. For a virtual machine, you may manage the guest operating system. A managed database moves some maintenance to the provider while leaving your data-access configuration with you.

Read the chosen service's actual responsibility description. “In the cloud” is not a complete security design.

### Identify every credential

Identity and access management, or IAM, controls which users and workloads may do what. A workload is a running service or job, not necessarily a person. Prefer appropriately scoped short-lived identity mechanisms where available instead of copying broad permanent keys into code.

### Keep private data private

Check storage exposure, network access and object permissions separately. A private network does not make an overly powerful application identity harmless. An encrypted object can still be readable by an unintended account with the key permissions.

### Prepare for change and recovery

Record configuration changes, administrative actions and billing/resource limits. Plan how to revoke access and recover data. Verify the intended denied cases using fictional diagrams or the approved lab; do not infer security solely from a console's green status indicator.
example:
Provider-neutral teaching policy
Workload W may read bucket training-notes objects under prefix public/.
W may not write objects or read private/.
Assume this policy is the sole grant; default deny.
W read public/intro.txt -> allow
W read private/note.txt -> deny
W write public/new.txt -> deny
explanation: The sole-grant assumption makes the fixture determinate. A real account may inherit another grant, so effective access must include all applicable policy. A cloud access key copied into a frontend bundle would be visible to users; use only intentionally public client configuration there.
exercise: Evaluate the three supplied requests plus W deleting public/intro.txt. Then use this invented managed-database contract, not a real provider claim: provider patches physical hosts, host OS and database engine; customer manages users, data permissions and application code; provider performs scheduled backups only when customer enables/configures them; customer chooses retention and tests restore. Assign responsibility for data access, engine patching, backup configuration, backup execution and restore testing. No account or paid service is required.
solution: Read public/intro.txt allows; read private/note.txt, write public/new.txt and delete public/intro.txt all deny because the sole grant is read under public/. Under the invented contract, customer owns data-access policy, backup configuration/retention and restore testing; provider owns host/engine patching and execution of enabled scheduled backups. Execution and configuration are separate duties. For a real service, replace these assumptions with its current documented contract and deployed settings.
challenge: Design a least-privilege identity for a read-only report worker. State allowed resources/actions, credential lifetime, revocation/recovery and a negative permission test. Explain how you would verify the deployed binding.
challenge_solution: Example paper policy: report-worker may read only the designated report-input prefix and return the report through the approved caller channel without writing to that input store; it cannot delete inputs or administer accounts. Prefer the platform’s scoped workload identity and short-lived credentials, with documented disable/revoke and job-recovery steps. Positive check reads an authorised synthetic input; negative checks deny another dataset and an input deletion. Inspect the actual deployed workload identity, role attachment and effective policy, then record observations from designated resources. A checked-in policy alone does not prove its deployment.
